title: The meaning of default options for potential organ donors
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: Rates of participation in organ donation programs are known to be powerfully influenced by the relevant default policy in effect ("opt-in" vs. "opt-out"). Three studies provide evidence that this difference in participation may occur in part because the requirement to opt-in or opt-out results in large differences in the meaning that individuals attach to participation. American participants in Study 1 rated participation as a significantly more substantial action when agreement was purportedly obtained under opt-in rather than opt-out conditions, and nonagreement as a greater abrogation of responsibility when that decision was made under opt-out rather than under opt-in conditions. Study 2 replicated these findings with respondents who live in Germany, which employs an opt-in donation policy, and in Austria, which has an opt-out policy. Study 3 required American participants to rate various actions that differ in the effort and self-sacrifice they demand. As predicted, the placement of organ donation on the resulting multidimensional scaling dimension differed significantly depending on whether it purportedly was made in an opt-in country (where it was considered roughly akin to giving away half of one's wealth to charity upon one's death) or an opt-out country (where it fell between letting others get ahead of one in line and volunteering some time to help the poor). We discuss the relationship between this change of meaning account and two other mechanisms-behavioral inertia and implicit norms-that we believe underlie the default effect in decision making and other effects of policies designed to influence decision-makers.

claims.text: The requirement to opt-in or opt-out results in differences in the meaning individuals attach to organ donation participation.
Participants rate organ donation participation as a significantly more substantial action when agreement is purportedly obtained under opt-in rather than opt-out conditions.
Participants rate nonagreement to organ donation as a greater abrogation of responsibility when the decision is made under opt-out rather than opt-in conditions.
Differences in the perceived meaning of organ donation decisions between opt-in and opt-out defaults replicate among respondents living in Germany and Austria.
The placement of organ donation on a multidimensional scaling dimension of effort and self-sacrifice differs significantly depending on whether it purportedly occurs in an opt-in or opt-out country.
In an opt-in country framing, organ donation is evaluated as roughly akin to giving away half of one's wealth to charity upon death.
In an opt-out country framing, organ donation is evaluated as falling between letting others get ahead in line and volunteering time to help the poor.
A change of meaning account, behavioral inertia, and implicit norms underlie default effects in decision making.

methodologies.name: Perceived Meaning Rating Task (Study 1)
methodologies.description: American participants evaluated the substantiality of agreeing to donate and the abrogation of responsibility from nonagreement under opt-in versus opt-out conditions.

methodologies.name: Cross-National Replication Survey (Study 2)
methodologies.description: Survey replicating Study 1 measures among citizens residing in countries with contrasting real-world defaults.

methodologies.name: Multidimensional Scaling of Effort and Self-Sacrifice (Study 3)
methodologies.description: American participants rated actions differing in effort and self-sacrifice to place organ donation along a derived dimension under opt-in versus opt-out frame.
